claims.claim: The "parse should fail given sparse array as tuple" test shows that testTuple.parse rejects a sparse array of the correct length (new Array(3)), so a length match alone is not sufficient for tuple parsing to succeed.

In these tests, a preprocess callback that calls ctx.addIssue without fatal:true still produces two issues total (the custom one plus a downstream type error), while setting fatal:true on the addIssue call reduces the result to exactly one issue.

The 'parse nonstrict object with unknown keys' test calls .parse() directly without wrapping it in expect(...).toThrow() or asserting on the returned value, so it only checks that parsing does not throw rather than verifying any output.

In the prototype-pollution test, parsing an object literal with a __proto__ key against a record schema silently drops that key rather than throwing or merging it, so obj1.a stays undefined instead of becoming "evil".

The "require" test builds a baseSchema and immediately discards it (`baseSchema;`), with every actual assertion about the .require() behavior commented out, so this test currently exercises no assertions and passes trivially regardless of whether .require() works.
safeParse does not catch errors thrown from inside a refine callback itself — such an error still propagates and causes safeParse to throw, rather than being captured as a failed-validation result.
z.void() accepts only `undefined` as valid input and throws on both `null` and an empty string, so it is not a permissive catch-all for "nothing".
The "--discriminatedUnion" CLI flag branch pushes datetimeBenchmarks.suites instead of discriminatedUnionBenchmarks.suites, so passing --discriminatedUnion actually runs the datetime benchmarks.

z.literal() accepts a Symbol value (not just primitive string/number/boolean literals), as shown by literalTerrificSymbol being created from a Symbol and successfully parsing that exact symbol instance.

This test performs no runtime assertions at all (no expect/toEqual calls); it only compiles a mapped-type computation and calls util.assertEqual, so the exhaustiveness check it performs happens purely at TypeScript compile time, not at test-run time.

flatten() routes an issue with an empty path entirely into formErrors (the schema-level refine failure lands as {formErrors: ["Must be equal"], fieldErrors: {}}) while any issue with a non-empty path is keyed into fieldErrors under its field name instead, as shown by the two contrasting expect(...).toEqual(...) blocks in the "all errors" test.

ipv4RegexB uniquely implements each octet alternation using lookahead assertions with backreferences (e.g. (?=(25[0-5]))\1) instead of plain grouped alternation used by the other candidate regexes in this benchmark.

When an array field fails both its element-type check and its min-length check at once, parsing does not stop at the first violation: the "continue parsing despite array size error" test shows the resulting error carries two issues rather than just one.

The DeepPartial conditional type only recurses into ZodObject, ZodArray, ZodOptional, ZodNullable and ZodTuple wrappers; any other ZodTypeAny falls through unchanged in the final ": T" branch instead of being deepened.

The too_small and too_big messages use type-specific wording rather than one shared template: strings get 'over'/'under' phrasing for the exclusive case while numbers and dates get 'greater than'/'less than' phrasing, so a caller cannot assume a uniform sentence shape across issue.type values.

The 'many' discriminatedUnion benchmark suite only exercises valid-parsing benchmarks for two of its four schema variants (a and c), never adding a corresponding 'valid: b' or 'valid: d' case even though dSchema and bSchema are both part of the union.

The format() method omits entries for array/tuple indices that did not fail validation entirely (e.g. error.inner?.name?.[1] is undefined), rather than including them as empty objects with an empty _errors array.
Scalars only permits a single flat array of primitives (Primitive[]), not arrays of arrays, since it is defined as Primitive | Primitive[] rather than a recursively nested type.

z.date().min()/.max() bounds are inclusive rather than exclusive: the "passing validations" test parses the exact benchmark boundary date successfully through both the min-checked and the max-checked schema.

The "min max getters" test shows that calling .min() or .max() a second time overwrites minValue/maxValue with the new bound (min(5).min(10) yields 10, max(5).max(1) yields 1) rather than combining them into the strictest bound.

Calling the synchronous .parse() on a schema built with an async .refine() callback is asserted to throw regardless of what the async check would eventually resolve to, since the first test throws even for a refine that resolves the Promise to true.

CastToStringTuple silently falls through to `never` for a non-string tuple result instead of constraining or erroring on the original type parameter, so UnionToTupleString resolves to `never` rather than producing a compile error when given a non-string union.

Parsing an empty object schema (z.object({}).safeParse({})) succeeds even when the global Date, Set, or Map constructors are deleted beforehand, showing that path does not internally depend on any of those three globals.

"promise parsing success 2" shows z.promise(...).parse() accepts a plain object that merely has then() and catch() methods (a thenable stub, not an actual Promise instance), so the schema validates by duck-typing rather than checking for a real Promise.

Every "invalid" benchmark case in this file wraps the parse call in a try/catch with a completely empty catch block, so the thrown validation error is silently discarded rather than inspected or asserted on.

For a promise schema, .readonly() leaves the inferred static type as plain Promise<string> (not wrapped in Readonly<...>) even though the "async object freezing" test shows the resolved value is actually Object.frozen at runtime after parseAsync — so the type signature does not reveal that freezing occurs.
This unit exports its own absolute source path as `filePath` by reading the ambient `__filename`, in addition to exporting the schema/type/instance fixtures used elsewhere.

In the generated People fixtures, `hair` and `active` are both derived from the same untouched counter value before any other field call increments it, so every generated person has hair 'blue' if and only if `active` is true, rather than being independently randomized fields.

addIssueToContext builds its errorMaps list in the order contextual, schema-bound, override, default, then reverses that array before iterating and letting each map's result overwrite errorMessage, so the contextual map actually wins as highest priority and the default map as lowest, the opposite of the array's declared order.

A single map entry that has both an invalid key and an invalid value produces two separate issues (one coded invalid_type at path [0,"key"], another at path [0,"value"]) rather than a single combined issue for that entry, as shown in the "invalid key and invalid input" test.

In the "break if dirty" test, once the leading refine on the string fails, the chained transform/pipe stages do not run and contribute no additional issues — both failing inputs end up with exactly one issue in the error, not one from each stage.

The base64 validator treats the empty string as valid input: the "base64 validations" test includes "" in validBase64Strings with an explicit comment noting it is technically valid base64, and asserts safeParse succeeds on it.
z.instanceof() accepts an abstract class constructor (AbstractBar) as its argument, and the resulting schema successfully parses instances of a concrete subclass (Bar) that extends it.

In the 'from const' test, GreekEnum accepts the numeric value 3 (Greek.Gamma) but throws on the unrelated number 2, showing nativeEnum matches only the object's actual member values rather than accepting any number when a numeric member is present.

The 'string params' test deliberately passes z.custom<number> a predicate that returns true precisely when x is NOT a number, inverting the expected check so that parsing a genuine number (1234) is what triggers the custom error message.
manySuite only benchmarks valid parses against schemas a and c, leaving the b and d members of the four-schema union never exercised by a valid-parse case.

For z.set(...), per-element validation issues carry a single-element path holding just the numeric index (e.g. path: [0], path: [1]), unlike the key/value-qualified paths used for maps, as shown in the "throws when the given set has multiple invalid entries" test.

The manual "capture groups + code" benchmark validates leap years with the full Gregorian rule (divisible by 4 and not by 100, or divisible by 400) rather than the simpler divisible-by-4-only check that the sibling regex-based leap-year variant appears to approximate.

isAborted/isDirty/isValid are verified against plain object literals with a `status` field rather than any constructed class instance, showing they classify a SyncParseReturnType purely by structural shape, not by identity or prototype checks.

In the 'short circuit on dirty' test, chaining .refine(() => false).transform(val => val.toUpperCase()) on invalid input (1234) does not throw a TypeError from calling toUpperCase on a non-string; the reported error is only the invalid_type issue, so the transform step's callback is effectively not surfaced as a second failure.
The 'optional string' and 'nullable string' benchmark cases only parse the `long` string value, never `empty` or `short`, unlike the base stringSchema which is benchmarked against all three lengths.
Only a single no-op test (test("", () => {})) actually executes in this file; every substantive Go-To-Definition/language-server test is commented out and does not run.

"invalid array merge" shows z.intersection() can still fail with an invalid_intersection_types issue even when both branch schemas individually parse the input successfully, because one branch's .transform() produces an extra element that makes the two branch outputs fail a deep-equality merge check.

Branding only affects a schema's output/inferred type, not its input type: z.input<typeof age> is asserted equal to plain number while z.infer<typeof age> is asserted distinct from it, so branded values are still accepted as plain, unbranded input.

In the "complex chain example" test, calling .removeCatch() strips only the catch it is chained directly after ('qwer'); an earlier .catch('asdf') placed before the transforms still silently substitutes on invalid input, so parsing an invalid value like 15 resolves to "ASDF!" instead of surfacing an error or falling through to the outermost .catch('asdfasdf').
getValidEnumValues filters an enum object's keys by checking whether obj[obj[k]] is not a number, which excludes the numeric reverse-mapping entries that TypeScript numeric enums generate.

Each suite's 'cycle' handler reads the suite's own name via `(emptySuite as any).name` / `(shortSuite as any).name` / `(longSuite as any).name`, casting to any because the Benchmark.Suite type used here does not expose a typed `name` property even though the constructor is called with a name string.

The 'chained defaults' test shows that stacking .default() calls does not layer them: z.string().default('inner').default('outer') parses undefined to 'outer', meaning only the last-applied default takes effect and the earlier one is discarded.
Calling .catchall() after .strict() overrides the strict unknown-keys rejection, so unknown keys are instead validated against the catchall schema rather than causing parse failure.

flatten() only keys fieldErrors by an issue's first path segment (sub.path[0]), discarding any deeper path segments, whereas format() in the same class walks the issue's full path array to build a nested tree — so the two error-shaping methods diverge in how they handle nested-object/array issue paths.

This codebase exposes two distinct APIs for defining a recursive schema, z.late.object(() => ({...})) and z.lazy(() => z.object({...})), and both are shown parsing the same recursive Category data successfully.

A description set via the constructor option survives being wrapped through a chain of .optional().nullable().default(...) — three different wrapper schema types stacked in sequence — not just a single wrapper.
The "mocker" test never calls expect on any of the accessed Mocker properties, so it only verifies that reading each getter does not throw rather than checking any produced value.

checkErrors is exercised against z.tuple([]) and z.unknown() in addition to the primitive types, asserting that wrapping any of these in .optional() leaves the formErrors produced for non-undefined bad input unchanged from the unwrapped schema's formErrors.

Calling .augment() a second time with a key that already exists overwrites that key's schema entirely rather than merging with it: `species` changes from z.string() to z.array(z.string()), and parsing confirms the object now requires an array for species, not a string.

Passing an explicit `false` for a key in .pick()/.omit() (e.g. { name: true, age: false }) is flagged by TypeScript as a type error (@ts-expect-error) but is accepted at runtime and behaves identically to simply omitting that key, as the accompanying parse assertions confirm.

superRefine's callback can be typed as a type predicate (arg is X), and the test confirms this actually narrows the value's static type for subsequent chained .refine/.superRefine calls in the same chain, not just for code after the whole chain resolves.

In the "nested no undefined" test, a union field built with z.string().or(z.array(z.string())) and placed on an object without .optional() rejects `undefined` for that field, confirming a bare union member does not implicitly permit a missing/undefined value.

In the "min max getters" and "int getter" tests, every `.toBeNull` matcher is referenced without being called as a function (e.g. `expect(...).toBeNull;` instead of `expect(...).toBeNull();`), so those assertions never actually execute.

Every substantive test in this file (over twenty cases covering pick/omit masking behavior) is commented out; the only test that actually executes is `test("test", () => { z; })`, which performs no assertion and no parse call.

promiseSchema.safeParseAsync resolves with success:true even when the wrapped promise will eventually resolve to invalid data; the ZodError only surfaces later when the caller awaits the returned data promise, which then rejects.

errToObj and toString handle an undefined message asymmetrically: errToObj falls back to an empty object {}, while toString falls back to undefined itself (via optional chaining on message?.message) rather than to an empty string.
z.coerce.bigint() failures throw plain (non-ZodError) errors on invalid input, unlike z.coerce.string/number/boolean/date whose failures the same file marks as throwing z.ZodError.

The "parse dateSchema invalid date" test wraps its only assertion inside a try/catch with no code path outside the catch block, so if parseAsync(new Date("invalid")) did not reject, the catch would never run and the test would still pass without ever checking the invalid_date issue code.

Unlike the other getters (string, number, bigint, boolean, date), which each recompute a fresh random value on every access, the `symbol` getter always returns the same module-level `testSymbol` instance, so successive calls to `.symbol` are reference-equal.

The 'parse' test calls crazySchema.parse() on a complex object with no wrapping expect() or assertion on the return value afterward, so it only verifies that parsing does not throw rather than checking any parsed output.

Every validation test in this file wraps its parseAsync call and expect() assertions inside a try/catch with no assertion outside the catch block and no fail()/expect.assertions call, so a test passes vacuously without checking anything if the parse unexpectedly resolves instead of rejecting.

The "enum and nativeEnum" test shows discriminatedUnion's discriminator branches are not restricted to z.literal(...) values — z.enum(["b","c"]) and z.nativeEnum(MyEnum) are also accepted as the discriminator schema for a branch and successfully discriminate multiple raw values.
When every option in a union fails, the reported error is a single synthesized issue with code "custom", message "Invalid input", and an empty path — not each branch's own distinct validation error.

Despite its name "test this binding", the test never extracts or passes an unbound reference to an existing schema's safeParse method; each callback invocation constructs a brand-new z.string() and calls safeParse on it directly, so the test does not actually exercise `this`-binding behavior of a detached method.

The "allow extra parameters" test shows a function schema built with only `.args(z.string())` still accepts and ignores additional unvalidated arguments at call time, since implement((str, _arg, _qewr) => ...) is used directly as an Array.filter callback that also receives index and array.

ZodString's trim(), toLowerCase(), and toUpperCase() methods each construct `new ZodString({...this._def, checks: [...this._def.checks, {kind: ...}]})` directly, duplicating the exact logic of the `_addCheck` helper instead of calling `this._addCheck(...)` as every other check-adding method (email, url, min, max, regex, etc.) does.

Excluding every value from an enum (FoodEnum.exclude(foods)) produces a runtime EmptyFoodEnum whose type does not actually equal z.ZodEnum<[]> — that specific assertion is marked @ts-expect-error — even though its inferred value type still correctly resolves to `never`.

overrideErrorMap is a single module-level mutable variable, so calling setErrorMap replaces the error map globally for every subsequent getErrorMap() call rather than being scoped to a particular schema or parse call.

crazySchema's `nonstrict` field is built with the `.nonstrict()` method (not `.passthrough()` or `.strict()`), showing that `.nonstrict()` is still a live, callable method on ZodObject at this version rather than an API that has been removed.

deepPartial() does not preserve array-level constraints like .min(42): the test itself asserts that safeParse({ array: [] }) succeeds (success === true) on a deep-partialed schema whose array field was declared with min(42), even though an empty array should fail that minimum.
